title: Refactoring Code Through Library Design
claim: Scattered, near-duplicate code across separate sources can be distilled into one shared library that the sources then import.
layout: Left-to-right: 3 source files, arrow, library with colored links back to sources
description: The figure reads left to right. On the left, a rounded box holds three file cards labeled File 1, File 2 and File 3, each with a GitHub icon. Each card has colored code blocks: blue for similar functions, red for similar classes, green for similar functions. Colored captions sit under the box: blue 'Similar Functions', red 'Similar Classes', green 'Similar Functions'. A thick black arrow in the middle is labeled 'Distill Abstractions' above and 'Rewrite Sources' below. On the right, a 'LIBRARY' card holds three consolidated blocks, labeled Func A (blue), Class A (red) and Func B (green), under an 'import ...' header. Blue, red and green lines run from these blocks to rewritten Source cards on the right. In those cards the duplicated code is replaced by short colored lines. The eye goes first to the colored blocks and the arrow.
caption: Overview of the refactoring problem. A refactoring task comprises a set of \ITEM{}s. We refactor the \ITEM{}s by designing a new library. Candidate refactorings are evaluated based on a refactoring metric, and are expected to maintain correctness of the original code sources (pass rate). We explore several refactoring metrics in this paper.
abstract: Maintainable and general software allows developers to build robust applications efficiently, yet achieving these qualities often requires refactoring specialized solutions into reusable components. This challenge becomes particularly relevant as code agents are increasingly used to solve isolated one-off programming problems. We investigate code agents' capacity to refactor code in ways that support consolidation and reusability. We first investigate what makes a good refactoring, finding via simulation results and a human study that proxies of program size, such as Minimum Description Length, better predict preferable refactorings than extant software engineering metrics, such as Maintainability Index. We then present \textsc{Librarian}, a method that combines divide-and-conquer with sample-and-rerank to generate reusable libraries. We compare \textsc{Librarian} to state-of-the-art library generation methods, and study it on real-world Python programs.
